stories.extended_summary: Joseph Phillips After more than 30 years as the capital’s professional ballet company, Columbia Classical Ballet is opening its own school. The School of Columbia Classical Ballet will open September 8 at 610 Harden Street in Five Points, where children ages three through 18 will train in the same studios as the professional company, taught by the dancers and coaches who perform with it. The studio sits behind a wall of glass on the street. Anyone can stop at the window and watch professional dancers at work, free, every day. Starting August 31, the company will take class every weekday morning at 10 a.m. in full view of the sidewalk. Five Points has long been known for its nightlife. stories.summary: By Kai Curry NORTHWEST ASIAN WEEKLY Jet Lai (Photo provided by the Lai Family) Like most kids, 10-year-old Jet Lai has some trouble finishing his chores. Unlike most kids, Lai turned this into an opportunity. The inventive Whidbey Islander created an app that will tell parents when their kids really finish their chores. stories.extended_summary: By Kai Curry NORTHWEST ASIAN WEEKLY Jet Lai (Photo provided by the Lai Family) Like most kids, 10-year-old Jet Lai has some trouble finishing his chores. Unlike most kids, Lai turned this into an opportunity. The inventive Whidbey Islander created an app that will tell parents when their kids really finish their chores. Called “ChoreCheck,” this app uses current digital technology to determine whether tasks get done, and limits screen time until they do. Lai made it to the quarter finals of Bill Nye’s America’s Favorite Student with his digital skills, which are what led him to creating the app shortly afterward. Lai now fears he won’t make it through any other contests, because, as he says, only half-jokingly, “I’ll probably be America’s most hated student after this app gets published.”

stories.title: Flau’jae Johnson Returns To Savannah To Give Back
stories.summary: WNBA rookie Flau'jae Johnson came back to her hometown Savannah to host her fourth annual Back to School Giveback, hooking up thousands of students with free backpacks, supplies, haircuts, and more. The event hit full capacity, proving the power of showing up for your community.
stories.extended_summary: The arena was packed as Savannah students grabbed free backpacks, fresh kicks, and fresh cuts — all thanks to WNBA rookie Flau'jae Johnson, who could've been anywhere but chose her hometown. Her More To 4 foundation threw its biggest Back to School Giveback yet, complete with games, food, and resources, getting kids hyped and ready for the year. Johnson, a Seattle Storm guard, knows a fresh fit and supplies can change everything for a kid facing the new school year. With thousands in attendance and sponsors like PUMA and e.l.f. behind her, she's proving that growing up in Savannah doesn't limit what you can become — it's exactly what you need. "They need to see me out here," she said, and they clearly do.

stories.title: Gorham Middle School Students Support Sustainability and Dignity with Thrift Shop
stories.summary: Two eighth graders turned a small idea into Rams Rack, a student-run thrift store inside Gorham Middle School offering free clothes and resources. Since opening, over 253 items have found new homes, giving peers both style and dignity.
stories.extended_summary: What started as a brainstorm after volunteering at Maine Needs is now a full-on boutique inside Gorham Middle School. Eighth graders Rataj and Leela pitched their vision for a stigma-free thrift store to school leaders, and then built it from the ground up — cleaning an old library space, collecting donations, even designing a logo with a local artist. Rams Rack has already moved 253+ pieces, giving students access to clothes they need without any shame. "Some love the sustainability, some love the find," but for those who need it, the store provides real dignity. All because two students saw compassion and spread it.

stories.title: Kosher dining pops up in Jackson Hole for the summer
stories.summary: Jackson Hole, a remote mountain town, just got its first-ever kosher restaurant this summer. Three rabbinical students drove from Brooklyn to make it happen, serving hundreds of meals to visitors from around the world.
stories.extended_summary: Deep in the Wyoming mountains, where celebrities go to escape, there was one thing you couldn't find: freshly prepared kosher food. For 20 years, the only option was Rabbi Mendelsohn's kitchen. So three rabbinical students packed up from Brooklyn and set up the Kosher Jackson Hole Grill, spending nearly 100 hours on logistics before they even opened. By mid-July, they'd dished out hundreds of meals to visitors from over a dozen countries — plus locals who'd never had the option. It's a summer pop-up that's about way more than food: it's a mitzvah, a lifeline, and a reminder that remote doesn't have to mean unreachable.

stories.title: Lake Country Faces: Cleaning up - Pequot Lakes teen builds trash can-cleaning company
stories.summary: Pequot Lakes teen Wyatt Verville turned a late-night idea into Clean Can Co., a pressure-washing business focused on trash cans. The side hustle exploded this summer, with a partnership with a local sanitation company making it boom.
stories.extended_summary: Most high schoolers spend summer at the lake — Wyatt Verville spends it blasting grime off garbage cans. The Pequot Lakes junior launched Clean Can Co. after realizing nobody in the Brainerd area did trash can cleaning. What started as a few word-of-mouth jobs and door hangers turned into a full-on business thanks to a partnership with Pequot/Gull Lake Sanitation. Now he runs the whole operation solo — intake forms, calls, the actual cleaning, all of it. "This summer is really the summer it took off," he says. With an entrepreneurial dad behind him, Wyatt's proving the best business ideas can come from the stinkiest places.

stories.title: Little Words Project Founder Turned Pain Into Power With Her Bracelet Brand
stories.summary: Adriana Carrig turned years of bullying into Little Words Project, a bracelet brand that sells uplifting words like "Worthy" and "You are enough." Since 2013, they've sold over 1 million bracelets and opened 11 stores, including one at Disney World.
stories.extended_summary: She was called "alien" and "spic" in middle school, and the pain lasted for years. But Adriana Carrig didn't let the words break her — she built a business to fight them. Little Words Project sells friendship bracelets stamped with positive messages, turning her trauma into a tool for self-love and connection. Since 2013, the brand has gone from a small idea to over 1 million bracelets sold, with stores from Manhattan to Disney World. Now, instead of the bullying that once consumed her, Carrig says her focus is on the positives that came from the pain. Her words are doing the opposite of what they used to.

stories.title: Manna Bakery Set to Open Thursday
stories.summary: After years selling out at farmers markets and pop-ups, Saif Manna is finally opening Manna Bakery, a brick-and-mortar spot in Fishtown. The buns, manakeesh, and Basque cheesecake he's famous for are about to have a permanent home.
stories.extended_summary: Cookies made for a girlfriend during lockdown turned into one of Philly's most beloved bakeries. Saif Manna started selling in his apartment, then popped up at cafes and markets, where lines would wrap around and 800 pastries would vanish in three hours. Now, after years of hustling and a team built for speed, Manna Bakery opens its first permanent location in Fishtown. The menu: Palestinian and Levantine classics like manakeesh, chicken and sumac buns, plus his viral Basque cheesecake and chewy chocolate chip cookies. It's the flavors of his family's tables, finally settling down — and locals couldn't be more ready.

stories.title: Miracle Marlie and her miracle mom
stories.summary: When Dami Quinones started an Instagram page to update family on her premature daughter's medical journey, she never imagined it would become a lifeline. Over 300 strangers crowdfunded Marlie's brain surgery, proving the power of a village built online.
stories.extended_summary: A tiny, four-months-premature baby, a terrifying brain surgery, and more than 300 strangers who paid for it. Dami Quinones, 25, started @MiracleMarlie during COVID because she was isolated and alone, hoping just to keep loved ones in the loop. Instead, the page became a community of other medical moms, a resource hub, and ultimately a fundraising miracle. Two years after Marlie's birth and months of hospital battles, strangers rallied to cover a surgery that changed everything. For Quinones, it's proof that "it takes a village" — even if that village is online.

stories.title: Montana Teen Uses Rodeo Lasso to Rescue Drowning Man on Yellowstone River
stories.summary: A 14-year-old Montana ranch kid used his lasso to rescue a drowning man from the Yellowstone River, catching him around the arm and neck like a true cowboy. The rescue took just three minutes from the 911 call.
stories.extended_summary: A 14-year-old who spends afternoons roping a dummy became the hero of a real-life Western. Jory Thomas was at his grandparents' place on the Yellowstone River when a raft hit a bridge pier and sent four people into the water. Three made it to shore; one guy was being swept away, clinging to a cooler. Without thinking, Jory waded in chest-deep with his lariat and — on the first try — looped the man around the arm and neck, then reeled him in with help from a bystander. His dad, a volunteer firefighter, had already called 911. From first scream to rescue: just 3 minutes. Talk about stop, drop, and rope.

stories.title: OHSU nursing student designs program to assess health needs in Baker School District
stories.summary: Reno Hammond, a nursing student, built a better way to assess health needs for the 1,500 students in Baker School District. His spreadsheet-based system replaces a clunky form, giving school nurses a clear picture before issues become emergencies.
stories.extended_summary: For school nurses Riley Hall and Hailey Siddoway, the old health assessment system was a headache: an online form only a third of families filled out, with info scattered across paper and pixels. Enter Reno Hammond, a Baker High grad now in OHSU's nursing program. His challenge: find a better way. He taught himself advanced spreadsheets, compiled evidence-based tools, and created a layered system that lets nurses see severe health needs at a glance — instead of digging through files one student at a time. It's not flashy, but for 1,500 kids, it could be a game-changer. Hammond calls the self-learning part "a lot," but the result speaks for itself.

stories.title: New art gallery creates sense of belonging for Detroit’s Caribbean community
stories.summary: After a decade of day jobs, Detroit artist Dior Leggette won Art of the Mix and landed a Reebok collab — just as art curator Dion Walcott's new gallery gave Caribbean creatives a place to belong.
stories.extended_summary: When Dior Leggette walked into Art of the Mix, she was ready to give up on her creative dream. The Detroit muralist had spent 10 years designing custom sneakers while working retail, unsure if she'd ever get a bigger platform. Then she won the competition — her design will hit stores as a Reebok release. Her victory came through Martk'd, the creative agency behind the new Art and Belonging Martkt gallery in Midtown, which is giving Black and Brown artists the opportunities Leggette thought were out of reach. For her, it felt like divine confirmation: "This is where you're supposed to be."

stories.title: On the Blackfeet Reservation, families learn to search for their own missing relatives
stories.summary: A new training program on the Blackfeet Reservation teaches families how to search for missing loved ones — filling a gap left by under-resourced law enforcement.
stories.extended_summary: When someone goes missing on tribal land, families often have to search themselves. Law enforcement is stretched thin, and legal jurisdiction gets complicated, leaving communities without answers. Haley Omeasoo founded Ohkomi Forensics to change that. Her two-day training, led with University of Montana graduate students, teaches community members how to organize searches, stay safe, and even identify human remains if recovery becomes necessary. It's a skill that turns grief and frustration into action — and gives families the tools and confidence to bring their relatives home.

stories.title: One toothbrush at a time — Local brothers build nonprofit to improve children’s oral health
stories.summary: Brothers Mikey and Marcus Kang started Bright Start Initiative to give every kid access to toothbrushes and dental education — and they're going nationwide with 25,000 kits.
stories.extended_summary: As sons of dentists, Mikey and Marcus Kang never thought twice about having a toothbrush. But they realized many kids across Washington don't — and that bothered them. So the Newport High School students created Bright Start Initiative, a nonprofit that hands out dental care kits to elementary students and offers multilingual resources in 18 languages. Last year, they distributed 6,880 kits. This year, they're aiming for 25,000 nationwide, plus 300 monthly kits to people experiencing homelessness in four cities. For the Kang brothers, reaching immigrant families is personal: their own family came from Korea, and they know what it's like to face barriers without information.

stories.title: She Was Terrified of Sharks, Now She Has 108 Shark Tattoo
stories.summary: After Jaws scared her as a kid, Emily Morrison became a shark biologist with a Guinness World Record — 108 shark tattoos and a mission to replace fear with fascination.
stories.extended_summary: Emily Morrison was convinced a shark would eat her after watching Jaws at age 8. Instead of running from that fear, she dove into it — studying sharks, building a career as a biologist and educator, and eventually marking her journey through ink. She holds the Guinness World Record for most shark tattoos on a woman's body, now at 108 species and fossil designs, including a real shark tooth. This Shark Week, she added two new tattoos on camera for Discovery's "My Strange Shark Addiction." But the ink isn't just for looks: every tattoo represents her mission to teach people that sharks deserve awe, not panic.

stories.title: Survivor of human trafficking in Elyria now a fierce advocate for other survivors: Part 2
stories.summary: After surviving 11 years of trafficking, Brittany Figlar escaped, helped convict her trafficker, and now fights for other survivors across Ohio.
stories.extended_summary: Brittany Figlar spent 11 years trapped in sex trafficking, abused and ignored by the system meant to protect her. She survived a jail bench warrant, forced drug dependency, and a final trafficker's trap — before escaping completely and getting clean. In court, her testimony helped put her trafficker behind bars for life. Today, Figlar is a fierce advocate for survivors in Northeast Ohio, using her story to push for change and support others still finding their way out. Her journey from victim to advocate is proof that survival isn't the end of the story — it's the beginning.

stories.title: Temple Shalom Introduced Him to Judaism. Now He’s in Rabbinical School.
stories.summary: Simon Blechman discovered his great-grandparents were Jewish, converted with help from Temple Shalom, and is now heading to rabbinical school.
stories.extended_summary: Simon Blechman grew up not knowing about his family's Jewish roots. Then a casual question to his grandfather revealed his great-grandparents were Jewish — a fact his grandfather didn't think mattered. Blechman found it transformative. He started learning, visited Temple Shalom on a whim, and was greeted so warmly that he never left. Rabbi Rachel Ackerman helped him enroll in conversion classes, and Cantor Ze'evi Tovlev guided him toward Hebrew Union College. Now he's part of the school's largest rabbinical cohort in over a decade — all because a congregation made a stranger feel like family.

stories.title: The Rise of the Dad Club
stories.summary: A Brooklyn dad's call to meet other first-time dads turned into the Brooklyn Stroll Club, a movement redefining modern fatherhood across the country.
stories.extended_summary: When Joe Gonzales became a dad, he was overwhelmed with doubts — even worrying strangers would think he'd "stolen" his own baby. So he posted a call for other new dads in Brooklyn to meet at McCarren Park. A few guys showed up, sat around, and talked without pride. That gathering became the Brooklyn Stroll Club, now a thriving community where dads share the scary and confusing parts of parenting. Gonzales says being a present parent is the small thing that builds a better community. From Brooklyn, similar dad clubs are popping up nationwide — proof that fatherhood isn't about doing it alone.

stories.title: Tiny Threads of Love throws inaugural Back-to-School Community Cookout and Field Day
stories.summary: At 19, Anigha Johnson started Tiny Threads of Love and just threw her first back-to-school cookout, handing out 207 filled book bags to kids in Marlboro County.
stories.extended_summary: Anigha Johnson isn't your average 19-year-old. She founded Tiny Threads of Love to lift up her South Carolina community, and on Saturday, the organization hosted its first Community Cookout, Field Day, and Back-to-School Bash. 207 book bags packed with supplies and dental care went to local students, alongside food, games, and support from vendors. Her cousin even flew down from Boston to cheer her on. Johnson's goal is bigger than one event: she wants to connect families with housing, food, and resources. "I just want to help children and families in need" — and she's already making that happen.

stories.extended_summary: More than 200 people gathered at Wilson Park on the city’s Southside on Saturday as cars whizzed past over their heads. For the sixth year in a row, the park nestled between Interstate 81 and Pioneer Homes played host to Syracuse police officer Brandon Hanks’ and Syracuse Housing Authority’s 10K basketball tournament. stories.title: Florida Shelter Celebrates 11-Year-Old Boy for Spending Over 100 Hours Reading to Rescue Pets
stories.summary: Eleven-year-old Nehemiah Turner is the first volunteer to log 100 hours reading to rescue pets — and he's making shelter animals feel loved.
stories.extended_summary: Nehemiah Turner loves reading, and he loves animals. So he combined both at the Jacksonville Humane Society's Pawsitive Reading program, where kids read aloud to shelter pets. The animals get comfort from a calm, friendly voice, and the kids practice literacy — a win-win. Nehemiah just became the program's first volunteer to hit 100 hours, a milestone the shelter celebrated with a big shout-out. It's a sweet reminder that even a small act — sitting and reading with a nervous pup — can change an animal's whole day. Nehemiah's commitment proves you're never too young to make a difference.

Tomi Love and her wife, Jasmine Lazaro, are both registered nurses who created The People’s Medic to provide free first-aid educ
stories.extended_summary: Down in the Historic Westside, behind a mosque, stand two tents and an RV that operate a medical clinic for unhoused individuals every week. With limited equipment and a volunteer system, The People’s Medic supplies medical care to Las Vegas’ most vulnerable communities. After working in hospitals for over five years, they both decided to take health care into their own hands.
